author: A Robot
objectives: Identify the structural components of DNA and describe how they assemble into the double helix.
Apply complementary base-pairing rules (A-T, G-C) and explain the hydrogen-bond basis for pairing specificity.
Describe the antiparallel, 5'-to-3' orientation of the two DNA strands and its chemical basis.
Trace the roles of helicase, single-strand binding proteins, DNA polymerase, and DNA ligase at the replication fork.
Explain the leading/lagging strand asymmetry and Okazaki fragment formation as a consequence of antiparallel template strands.
Articulate why DNA replication is semiconservative and predict daughter molecule composition across replication rounds.

modules.description: Introduces DNA as a schematic ladder diagram showing the sugar-phosphate backbones and color-coded base pairs.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify the sugar-phosphate backbone and nitrogenous bases in a simplified DNA schematic.
Recognize the four bases by their color code and one-letter abbreviations.
instructions: Observe the ladder structure as it is built and labeled.

components.text: DNA: A Ladder of Base Pairs

clips.changeMeaning: Initial reveal of the two backbones as vertical lines, establishing the ladder framework before any bases are shown.
clips.narration: DNA is a polymer with a remarkably regular structure. Two sugar-phosphate backbones run alongside each other, connected by rungs made of paired nitrogenous bases.

clips.changeMeaning: Rungs are colored and labeled to show base identity, teaching the color code for A, T, G, and C base pairs.
clips.narration: Each rung is made of two bases meeting in the middle: adenine in red, thymine in blue, guanine in yellow, cytosine in green. Notice how each base only pairs with one partner.

modules.description: The flat ladder twists into the realistic double-helix geometry, letting students toggle between schematic and realistic views.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Map the schematic ladder representation onto the realistic helical geometry of DNA.
Recognize the helical turn periodicity of approximately ten base pairs per turn.
instructions: Use the toggle to switch between schematic and helical views.

clips.changeMeaning: The flat helix model rotates into its twisted double-helix form, animating the transition from schematic to realistic geometry.
clips.narration: Now watch as the flat ladder twists into its real three-dimensional shape: the double helix. The backbones spiral around a shared axis, and the base pairs stack like steps on the interior.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduces the toggle button affordance and highlights the ten-base-pair turn periodicity, reinforcing the ladder-to-helix mapping.
clips.narration: One full turn of the helix spans about ten base pairs. You can toggle between the schematic ladder and this realistic helix at any time to build your mental map between the two views.

modules.description: Displays directional arrows and 5'/3' labels on the helix to teach antiparallel orientation.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Describe the antiparallel orientation of the two DNA strands.
Explain how 5'-to-3' directionality of the backbone forces the antiparallel arrangement.
instructions: Rotate the helix to confirm the direction arrows from any angle.

clips.changeMeaning: Direction arrows and 5'/3' end labels appear on the helix, visually establishing the antiparallel orientation of the two strands.
clips.narration: Arrows along each backbone show the direction of the strand: one points up, the other points down. These directions refer to the carbon atoms of the sugar ring at each end.

clips.changeMeaning: Enables free rotation/dragging of the helix so students can confirm the antiparallel arrow pattern from multiple viewing angles.
clips.narration: The two strands always run in opposite directions. This antiparallel arrangement isn't optional — it's forced by the directional chemistry of the sugar-phosphate backbone. Try rotating the helix to confirm the arrows from any angle.

modules.description: An interactive drag-and-drop activity where students complete a complementary DNA strand.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Apply complementary base-pairing rules to construct a complementary strand.
Relate hydrogen bond count (2 for A-T, 3 for G-C) to base pair identity and stability.
instructions: Drag bases from the palette to complete the complementary strand on the right.

clips.changeMeaning: Reveals the template strand with its labeled sequence and an empty complementary backbone alongside a draggable base palette, setting up the interactive pairing task.
clips.narration: Here is a template strand reading 5' to 3': A-T-G-C-C-A-G-T. On the right is an empty backbone waiting for its complementary bases. Drag bases from the palette below to complete the pairing — remember, A pairs with T, and G pairs with C.

clips.changeMeaning: After correct placements, displays the completed complementary sequence label and hydrogen-bond dashed lines, confirming successful base pairing and reinforcing bond-count concept.
clips.narration: Well done — the completed strand reads 3'-TACGGTCA-5', running opposite to the template. Notice that A-T pairs form two hydrogen bonds while G-C pairs form three, making G-C pairs slightly stronger.

modules.description: Introduces helicase as it moves along the DNA, unwinding the double helix at the replication fork.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify helicase and describe its function of unwinding the double helix by breaking hydrogen bonds between base pairs.
instructions: Watch helicase move along the DNA and observe the strands separating.

clips.changeMeaning: Helicase enzyme appears at the top of the helix and begins moving downward, unwinding the strands as it travels to demonstrate its unwinding function.
clips.narration: Meet helicase, the first enzyme at the replication fork. It breaks the hydrogen bonds between paired bases, unwinding the double helix and exposing the two strands so they can serve as templates.

modules.description: SSBs attach to the separated strands behind helicase to keep them open and stable.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Explain the role of single-strand binding proteins in stabilizing exposed single-stranded DNA during replication.
instructions: Observe SSBs attaching to the strands as helicase continues unwinding.

clips.changeMeaning: Small SSB spheres appear attached along both separated strands behind the moving helicase, illustrating strand stabilization.
clips.narration: As helicase separates the strands, single-strand binding proteins, or SSBs, attach behind it. Single strands of DNA are unstable and tend to re-pair or fold on themselves — the SSBs hold them open and accessible for replication.

modules.description: DNA polymerase synthesizes the leading strand continuously, following the replication fork.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Explain why DNA polymerase synthesizes the leading strand continuously in the 5'-to-3' direction, moving with the replication fork.
instructions: Watch the leading strand grow continuously alongside the moving fork.

clips.changeMeaning: Polymerase appears on the leading-strand template and begins continuous elongation, growing the new complementary strand alongside the fork's movement.
clips.narration: DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to the 3' end of a growing strand, so it travels along its template in the 3'-to-5' direction, building the new strand 5' to 3'. On this template, that direction matches the moving fork — so polymerase can synthesize continuously. It needs a starting primer to begin, but once going, it doesn't stop.

modules.moduleName: Scene 8: Lagging Strand and Okazaki Fragments
modules.description: The lagging strand template is synthesized discontinuously as Okazaki fragments, later joined by DNA ligase.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Explain why the lagging strand is synthesized discontinuously as Okazaki fragments.
Describe the role of DNA ligase in joining Okazaki fragments into a continuous strand.
instructions: Watch fragments form on the lagging strand and observe ligase sealing them together.

clips.changeMeaning: Three Okazaki fragments appear sequentially along the lagging-strand template, illustrating discontinuous synthesis moving opposite to the fork.
clips.narration: On this template, the fork moves away from polymerase's required direction of travel, so it can't synthesize continuously. Instead, it works backward in short bursts, producing Okazaki fragments, then jumps back near the fork to start the next fragment.

clips.changeMeaning: Ligase enzyme appears and moves along the fragments, visually sealing the junctions to form a continuous strand.
clips.narration: Now DNA ligase arrives and seals the gaps between the Okazaki fragments, joining them into one continuous lagging strand.

modules.description: All five replication components are shown together, actively operating on a rotatable full fork model with a summary panel.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify all five replication fork components by name and function.
Explain how the antiparallel structure of DNA forces the leading/lagging strand asymmetry.
instructions: Rotate the fork model and review the summary panel identifying each enzyme.

components.text:
Helicase: unwinds
SSBs: stabilize
Polymerase (leading): continuous
Polymerase (lagging): fragments
Ligase: seals fragments

clips.changeMeaning: The full replication fork model with all five components becomes visible and rotatable, alongside a summary panel labeling each enzyme's function, tying the asymmetry back to antiparallel structure.
clips.narration: Here is the complete replication fork: helicase unwinding at the front, SSBs holding the strands open, polymerase synthesizing the leading strand continuously, polymerase building Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand, and ligase sealing them behind. Because the two template strands run in opposite directions and polymerase can only build 5' to 3', the two new strands must be made differently. This asymmetry is a direct consequence of the antiparallel structure you saw earlier.

modules.description: A gold parental DNA molecule replicates across two rounds, with students predicting the composition of daughter molecules.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Explain why DNA replication is semiconservative.
Predict the strand composition of daughter molecules after one and two rounds of replication.
instructions: Predict the outcome of the second replication round before it plays out.

components.text: Predict round 2: (A) all half-gold/half-silver (B) two hybrid, two fully silver (C) all fully silver

clips.changeMeaning: The gold parental molecule splits into two daughter molecules, each recolored to show one gold (original) and one silver (new) strand, demonstrating semiconservative replication after round one.
clips.narration: This parental DNA molecule is rendered entirely in gold to mark the original material. Watch as it replicates: the strands separate, new complementary strands are synthesized in silver, producing two daughter molecules — each with one gold strand and one silver strand. This is what makes replication semiconservative: every daughter conserves one original parental strand.

clips.changeMeaning: Displays the prediction prompt with three answer options, pausing the scene for student input before round two of replication is revealed.
clips.narration: Now these two daughter molecules will each replicate again. Before we play it out — predict the composition of the four resulting molecules: will all four be half gold and half silver, will two be hybrid and two be fully silver, or will all four be fully silver?

clips.changeMeaning: Four granddaughter molecules appear, two colored as gold-silver hybrids and two as fully silver, revealing and confirming the correct prediction for round two of replication.
clips.narration: Here is round two: each daughter molecule separates and synthesizes a new silver strand. The result is four molecules — two are hybrids with one gold and one silver strand, and two are fully silver, containing no original parental material. This pattern of hybrid and fully-new molecules is exactly the signature that confirmed DNA replication is semiconservative rather than conservative or dispersive.

modules.description: A closing summary screen reviews the six core concept areas covered in the lab.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Summarize and integrate the six core concept areas: helix structure, base-pairing rules, antiparallel orientation, replication enzymes, leading/lagging strand asymmetry, and semiconservative replication.
instructions: Review the recap panel as each concept area is highlighted.

components.text:
1. Double-helix structure
2. Complementary base pairing
3. Antiparallel 5'-to-3' strands
4. Replication fork enzymes
5. Leading/lagging strand asymmetry
6. Semiconservative replication

clips.changeMeaning: Displays the full six-point recap panel summarizing all major concept areas covered across the lab as a final review.
clips.narration: Let's recap what we've covered: the double-helix structure with its sugar-phosphate backbones and bases; complementary base-pairing rules with hydrogen-bond counts; the antiparallel, 5'-to-3' arrangement of the two strands; the action of helicase, SSBs, polymerase, and ligase at the replication fork; the leading and lagging strand asymmetry with Okazaki fragments; and the semiconservative nature of replication.
